fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Ravid. I think about this a lot, because I spent most of my career on the vision side, and it's a little humbling.

The first thing I'd say is that it's not really that vision was around longer and failed. Vision actually kicked off the whole deep learning era, with AlexNet and ImageNet. For almost a decade, vision was where the architectures came from, where the scaling intuitions came from. But what we built in vision were tools. A classifier, a detector, a segmentation model. Each one solved a narrow task, each one needed its own labeled dataset, its own head, its own training recipe. If you wanted a new capability, you went back and built a new model. So the progress was real, but it was fragmented. It showed up as a feature inside a product, like photo tagging or face unlock, and nobody really thought of that as "AI" in the way people think of ChatGPT as AI.

Language is different in a few ways that I think compound on each other. One is that text comes with its own supervision. Next-token prediction is a task where the label is just the next word, so you get essentially unlimited training signal from the internet for free. In vision we spent years trying to find the equivalent self-supervised objective, and honestly it was much harder, because pixels are extremely redundant and the "right" thing to predict isn't obvious. Masked image modeling helped, contrastive learning helped, but none of it gave you the same clean scaling behavior that language had almost by accident.

The second thing is that language is the interface. When a model's input and output are both natural language, the task specification is just part of the input. You don't need a new head, you just ask. That's what unified everything. Suddenly one model is a translator, a coder, a summarizer, a tutor. In vision, even if your backbone was great, you still had to decide what the output format was, and that decision locked you into a task.

And the third is simply that language is what people use to think and communicate. A model that produces language is directly useful to a human sitting at a keyboard, without any engineering around it. That's why adoption was so fast. A vision model's output usually needs to be plugged into some larger system before it means anything to a person.

So my view is that vision got there first on the modeling side, but language had the better data, the better objective, and the better interface, and those three together are what produced the jump. The interesting part now is that vision is getting absorbed into that same paradigm, through vision-language models, and I think a lot of the lessons from the language side are finally coming back to us.

opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, because I come from the vision side. For most of the 2010s, vision was the flagship of deep learning. AlexNet, ResNet, all the architecture work happened on ImageNet. So it's a little humbling that language ended up driving the big jump.

I think there are a few reasons.

The first is the format of the task. In language, almost every problem can be written as text in, text out. Translation, summarization, question answering, coding, math: they're all the same interface. Once you train one model to predict the next token on a huge amount of text, you get a single system that can do all of them, and you just tell it what you want in natural language. Vision never had that. We had classification, detection, segmentation, depth estimation, each with its own output format, its own head, its own labeled dataset. The field was fragmented into many narrow tasks.

The second is the data and the objective. Text on the internet is already a highly compressed, abstract representation of human knowledge. Humans did the hard work of turning the world into concepts and reasoning before writing it down. So predicting the next word forces the model to learn something like world knowledge and reasoning. Pixels are much lower level and very redundant. If you predict the next pixel or reconstruct a masked patch, a lot of the signal is about texture and local statistics, not meaning. We've tried many self-supervised objectives in vision, and none has scaled as cleanly as next-token prediction.

The third is how people experience it. Vision models were very successful, but they were mostly invisible: face unlock, photo search, quality inspection in factories. They were components inside products. A chatbot is something you talk to directly, and anyone can use it with no training. That changed adoption a lot.

There's also a subtle point: the output of most vision systems was always language anyway. A class label is just a word from a small fixed vocabulary. In a sense, vision was bottlenecked by a tiny language interface. Once you connect vision to a language model, the output space becomes open-ended.

That said, I don't think vision is solved or less important. Current multimodal models still make surprisingly basic visual mistakes, like counting or spatial relations. So I think there's a lot of room for vision to catch up.

fable-5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think there are a few reasons, and it's something I've thought about a lot coming from the vision side.

The first is that language is just a much more universal interface. In computer vision, for a long time we built very task-specific systems — one model for classification, another for detection, another for segmentation. Each one needed its own labeled dataset, its own architecture tweaks, its own deployment pipeline. So even when vision models got really good, the value was locked inside narrow applications. With language models, a single model can do translation, summarization, coding, question answering, all through the same interface — you just type what you want. That generality is what made the jump feel so broad.

The second reason is data. Text on the internet is essentially a compressed record of human knowledge and reasoning. When you train a model to predict the next token on that data, you're implicitly teaching it facts, procedures, argument structures, even some reasoning patterns. Images, by contrast, mostly capture appearance. A photo of a cat tells you what a cat looks like, but it doesn't tell you much about the world's accumulated knowledge. So the supervision signal in text is just much richer per bit, in some sense, and it was available at enormous scale without human labeling.

And then there's the adoption side, which I think people underrate. Language is how humans naturally communicate, so a model that speaks language needs no special interface — anyone can use it immediately. Vision systems usually sit behind a product: they power your photo search or your car's driver assistance, and users never interact with the model directly. ChatGPT put the model itself in front of hundreds of millions of people, and that changed the public perception of what AI is.

The ironic thing is that a lot of the technical ingredients — large-scale pretraining, transfer learning, even transformers eventually — were being developed in vision too, and ideas flowed back and forth between the fields. But vision never had that single moment where capability, generality, and accessibility all lined up at once. Language did.

opus-5.text:
That's something I think about a lot, partly because I spent most of my career on the vision side.

I'd point to three things. The first is that text is the medium humans already use to express what they want. A vision model gives you a label, a box, a mask — those are useful, but someone still has to build a product around the output. With language, the output *is* the interface. You type a sentence, you get a sentence back, and suddenly the model is usable by a lawyer or a high school student with zero onboarding. Vision never had that moment where the raw model output was directly the thing a person wanted.

The second is the supervision signal. In vision we were stuck on human annotation for a long time. ImageNet was a thousand categories and an enormous labeling effort, and even when we moved to self-supervised learning — contrastive methods, masked autoencoders, I worked on some of this — the scaling payoff was never as dramatic. Text comes with its own objective for free. Every document on the internet is training data without anyone labeling anything. And I think the deeper point is that pixels are extremely redundant. Predicting the next patch of sky mostly teaches you about texture. Predicting the next word in a paragraph about, say, a legal argument forces you to model semantics and reasoning, because the information density per token is just so much higher. Language is already a compressed representation of human thought, and we got to train directly on the compression.

Third, and this is somewhat a sociological point: NLP unified on a single format. Everything became text-to-text. Translation, summarization, question answering, classification — one model, one loss. Vision stayed fragmented. Detection had its benchmarks, segmentation had its own, generation was a separate community. We were optimizing many narrow numbers instead of one general capability.

Though I'd push back a little on the framing. Vision did reach billions of people — it just did it invisibly, inside your phone camera and your photo search. And vision built a lot of the scaffolding that language models stand on: the GPU training stack, the architectural lessons, the whole cultural belief that scale works. The borrowing has gone both directions.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think there are a few reasons, and they stack on each other.

First, language is already a compressed form of human knowledge and reasoning. When you train on text, you're learning from what people chose to write down: facts, arguments, code, math, and instructions. Images are much more raw. A lot of pixels are redundant, and the semantic content per unit of data is lower. So next-token prediction on text gives you a very rich learning signal almost for free.

Second, language gives you a universal interface. With language models, one model and one training objective can handle translation, summarization, coding, question answering, and more, just by changing the prompt. In vision, we spent years building separate models for classification, detection, and segmentation. Those are important, but they're narrow, and the outputs, like a bounding box or a label, aren't something most people need in daily life.

Third, adoption is about usefulness to ordinary people. Anyone can type a question and get a useful answer, and that's a product experience people understood immediately. Vision systems were often embedded in the background, in a camera pipeline or a recommendation system, so people didn't directly feel them.

Finally, I think the scaling recipe just worked more cleanly for language. There was an enormous amount of text, a simple objective, and a very scalable architecture. Vision is catching up, but self-supervised learning there has been harder to turn into that same general-purpose capability.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to what the data already contains. Language is something humans have already compressed. Each token is a deliberate symbol, so learning to predict the next one forces a model to pick up grammar, facts, and patterns of reasoning. An image is mostly high-dimensional and redundant at the pixel level, and much of the signal is texture and lighting. Getting to semantics took a lot of effort, which is part of why vision leaned on carefully labeled datasets like ImageNet for so long.

The objective mattered too. Next-token prediction is simple, works on raw text at huge scale, and needs no labels. Once it was clear that the recipe kept improving predictably with more data and compute, the path forward was obvious. Vision had strong pretraining results as well, but its self-supervised methods were harder to make robust and general, so the field stayed closer to task-specific supervised models.

Then there's the interface. A text box that takes text and returns text is something anyone can use without knowing machine learning. Instruction tuning and preference training made these models follow what people actually wanted, so the jump from an impressive benchmark to a useful tool for everyday work happened quickly. Vision models were often excellent at one narrow task, like classification or detection, and that's much harder to package as a general assistant.

I don't think vision is behind in any fundamental way. I think we're seeing the consequences of which problem got the cleanest recipe first. Multimodal models are closing that gap, and I expect the next few years to look less like language versus vision and more like single models that do both well.

astra-6.text:
I think a big part of it is that language gives you both a way to learn about the world and a way to interact with the model. We use language to describe things, explain our reasoning, write instructions, write code. So learning to predict language can bring together many capabilities that we previously treated as separate tasks.

In computer vision, we often worked with a very specific setup: you have an image, and you want a category, or a bounding box, or a segmentation. Those are useful outputs, but turning them into something a person can use usually requires building a whole application around the model. With a language model, you can just ask for something. That makes the distance between a research capability and a useful product much shorter.

And the interaction is open-ended. You can ask a follow-up, correct the model, or give it an example of what you want. The same interface supports many different uses. So I would separate the capability jump from the adoption jump a little bit: language provides a rich learning signal, and conversation makes those capabilities accessible. Those two things reinforce each other.

sol-6.1.text:
I think language gives you a very general interface, both for learning and for using the model. So many things we want computers to do can be expressed in language. You can ask a question, describe a problem, give instructions, or ask for help writing code. That lets one model become useful in many different settings.

In computer vision, we made a lot of progress, but often the task was more specific: recognize an object, detect something in an image, produce a segmentation. To make that useful to somebody, you usually had to build an application around it. With a language model, the conversation itself can already be a useful application. People can try it immediately using an interface they understand.

There’s also something powerful about learning from language, because language contains explanations, relationships, and descriptions of how people solve problems. Learning to predict it can support a much broader set of behaviors than you might initially expect.

So I think the breadth of the capabilities and the accessibility reinforced each other. More people could discover useful things to do with the same system.

terra-5.6.text:
I think one big difference is that language is the interface to so much of human knowledge. Once you train on the internet, you are not just learning to recognize objects or categorize images—you are absorbing explanations, code, scientific text, conversations, and all these patterns of reasoning expressed in language. And then the interface is incredibly natural: anyone can just type a question or instruction.

Computer vision made huge progress, but many vision tasks were narrower and harder to deploy broadly. With language models, a single next-token prediction objective, enough scale, and a massive diverse dataset produced something that could generalize across many tasks without task-specific training. That combination—general capability plus an immediately usable interface—is what made the jump feel so broad.

sol-5.6.text:
I think language is a uniquely general interface. In computer vision, we often built a separate model, dataset, and output space for each task—classification, detection, segmentation, and so on. With language models, many tasks can be expressed in the same form: you describe what you want in natural language, and the model responds in natural language or code. That makes one model immediately useful for writing, programming, question answering, planning, and many other applications, often without retraining it.

There was also an enormous amount of text available on the internet, so scaling self-supervised learning exposed these models to a broad range of human knowledge and behavior. And from an adoption perspective, the interface is incredibly simple: anyone can open a chat box and start using it. Computer vision is often embedded inside a specialized system, whereas language models can interact directly with people and connect many different domains. I think that combination—scale, generality, and accessibility—is what produced such a broad jump.

luna-5.6.text: I think language became this unusually powerful interface between intelligence and the world. With vision, the model can recognize what is in an image, but language gives you access to knowledge, abstraction, planning, explanation, and interaction all at once. The training signal is also much richer: the internet provides enormous amounts of text, and next-token prediction turns that into a remarkably scalable form of self-supervision. Once transformers and large-scale compute made that work, the same model could be adapted to many different tasks just through prompting or a relatively small amount of fine-tuning. And the interface is incredibly accessible—people can use these systems in natural language, without learning a specialized tool. So the progress was not only a technical jump; it immediately translated into a general-purpose product that people could experiment with themselves.
